messages:
Sanjay: Quick question — proposing a KEK caching policy for envelope flows. We need to minimize KMS calls but still be able to rotate/revoke quickly. Thoughts? :thinking_face:
Laura: +1 we should balance latency and security. What are you imagining for cache granularity — per-process, per-pod, per-tenant?
Sanjay: Thinking per-service-instance (so per pod/container) with keys tagged by tenant-id when applicable. Cache stores plaintext DEK in memory, with the DEK wrapped by KEK stored in our DB. On request: fetch local DEK if present else call KMS GenerateDataKey.
Mike: Prefer GenerateDataKey over Encrypt/Decrypt where supported — that avoids an extra decrypt call when creating DEKs. But remember KMS quotas and spikes.
Ellie: Agreed. Also need rules for TTL and maximum lifetime of cached DEKs. If a KEK rotates we must not keep using old DEKs beyond their rewrap policy.
Sanjay: Proposed defaults: cache DEK plaintext in process memory for 15 minutes, max 1 hour with explicit rewrap check. Cache keyed by <key-id>:<dek-id>:<key-version>. On rewrap/rotation we invalidate by bumping key-version.
Laura: 15m default seems reasonable for latency. But for high-throughput services we might want longer TTL to avoid KMS thundering herd; maybe add jitter and an adaptive backoff.
Mike: Also implement a per-instance KMS token bucket so we don't blow past account-level KMS limits during startup. On cold start we can stagger calls with randomized delays.
Ellie: For incident scenarios (suspected key compromise) procedure should be: 1) disable KEK in KMS (or mark compromised), 2) trigger cluster-wide cache flush, 3) rotate to new KEK and rewrap DEKs asynchronously, 4) audit all KMS calls during window. Does that match ops expectations?
Sanjay: Yes. Important note: If KEK is disabled, instances that only have cached plaintext DEKs can continue issuing until their TTL expires. That's a tradeoff. We should document maximum window and provide an emergency short TTL mode to expedite revocation.
Laura: We should also support a 'panic rotate' mode where we proactively zero out process DEKs via a push invalidation (webhook/coordination). That requires CI/CD or control plane hooks to call a /flush endpoint with auth.
Mike: For audit logging — every GenerateDataKey/Decrypt/Encrypt call should include request context (service role, tenant-id, request-id). Send logs to our SIEM with KMS response metadata. Add synthetic digest of DEK rewraps so we can correlate rewrap events.
Ellie: RBAC: grant only the service role permission to GenerateDataKey and Encrypt/Decrypt for KEKs. Separate roles for admin (rotate) vs runtime. Key policies should disallow plaintext export except via KMS APIs we control.
Sanjay: Edge case: if KMS throttles, we need fallback behavior. Proposal: on throttling, retry with exponential backoff + jitter up to N tries, meanwhile serve from cache if DEK available. If no DEK, fail fast with clear error and circuit-breaker to avoid cascading retries.
Laura: Also add a metrics panel: KMS calls/sec, GenerateDataKey latencies, throttle/error rates, cache hit ratio, and number of in-memory DEKs. Alert on KMS error rate > 1% for 5m.
Mike: Implementation detail: store DEKs in protected heap (mmap + mlock where supported), zero memory on eviction. For container environments, ensure we set max heap and avoid swap so secrets don't leak to disk.
Ellie: For multi-cloud (AWS/GCP/Azure): abstract the key service behind an interface. Use provider-specific best practice: AWS GenerateDataKey, GCP's CMEK Encrypt + generateRandom for DEK, Azure wrapKey/unwrap. But keep same cache semantics.
Sanjay: Agreed. I'll draft a design doc with: cache TTL defaults, cache key format, rewrap/rotation protocol, RBAC policy snippet, and incident playbook.
Laura: One more thing — test plan: load test with KMS call spikes to verify token-bucket behavior and fallback. Also run red-team scenario for key compromise and measure time-to-revoke (TTRO).
Mike: Minor: include a per-tenant key-version header on wrapped DEK blobs so older clients don't accidentally use stale KEKs after rollout.
Ellie: Sounds good. Sanjay can you include example pseudocode for cache lookup + GenerateDataKey?
Sanjay: Sure — quick sketch:
```
// on request:
cache_key := fmt.Sprintf("%s:%s:%d", keyID, dekID, keyVersion)
if dek := cache.Get(cache_key); dek != nil { return dek }
// rate-limit KMS calls per-instance
if !kmsTokenBucket.Allow() { return error("kms throttled, no cached DEK") }
// prefer GenerateDataKey when available
resp := KMS.GenerateDataKey(KeyId=keyID, KeySpec="AES_256")
cache.Set(cache_key, resp.PlaintextDEK, ttl=15m + jitter())
storeWrappedDEK(dekID, resp.CiphertextBlob)
return resp.PlaintextDEK
```
Mike: Nice. Might add a rewrap worker that takes wrapped blobs and calls ReEncrypt/Encrypt to new KEK, updating DB and bumping keyVersion atomically.
Sanjay: Great feedback — I'll post the design doc in #eng-security later today and ping for reviews. :thumbsup:

Laura: Thanks everyone. If you spot gaps re: compliance (SOC2/GDPR) call them out in the doc — we need explicit retention and audit controls.
Mike: I'll review the RBAC snippets.
Ellie: I'll mock up the cache flush endpoint and an alert runbook.
